label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
@Kavya, I owe you an apology, and I want to offer that before correcting anything else.

I knew from day one that both candidates worked at SitterNest. I should have called you before we made the offers, not after. I’m sorry. You deserved a direct conversation, especially from someone you have helped as much as you have helped me.

Some details in your post are not accurate, and leaving them uncorrected will only make the story harder for both our teams.

We put a backend developer opening on DabbaDost’s LinkedIn page and Instahyre on 14 September. It was open to anyone. The first person applied on his own on 19 September. The second applied about two weeks later, referred by the first. Nobody from our side approached or DM’d either person.

The offers were 22% over their then-current CTC, not 40%. Both joined on 3 November. I’m sharing the number only because I don’t want 40% repeated as fact.

We also did not promise ESOPs we don’t have. Our pool is small, but it is real, documented, and on paper since January.

Two teammates leaving close together is hard for any early team, and I understand why you were upset. After the second offer was accepted, I messaged you on WhatsApp. When you didn’t reply, I should have called instead of leaving it there. But the bigger miss was earlier: I let the offers go out without giving you the courtesy of a call. That is on me.

This is not a public fight I want. You sat with me until 1 a.m. in the Koramangala office, fixing our Razorpay webhook mess before demo day. I have never forgotten that. We came through Foundry91 cohort 4 together, with demo day in March 2026, and your help has mattered to DabbaDost and to me.

We are 11 startups hiring from the same small talent pool in HSR and Koramangala. People will apply across our companies, and friends will refer friends. We cannot pretend that won’t happen, but we can handle it better.

My suggested cohort rule: if you are interviewing someone from another batch company, give that founder a heads-up before making an offer. Not to ask permission or block a move, but to show basic courtesy and avoid surprises.

Kavya, my respect for you is unchanged. If you’re okay with it, I’d like to buy you a coffee or get on a call this week, whenever suits you. I’d rather say the rest directly.
